name: Query federation / virtualization
use_case: One SQL over data left in place
description: Query federation inverts the usual pattern: instead of moving data into one store, a federation engine presents a single SQL interface over sources left where they are — operational databases, warehouses, lakes, even SaaS APIs — planning each query across connectors, pushing predicates down to the sources, and joining the results. It is the fastest way to answer cross-source questions and a pragmatic bridge during migrations or after acquisitions. The physics are honest: a federated join can never beat a local one, so mature deployments pair the engine with caching or materialization for the hot paths and treat federation as the long tail.
when_to_use: Answers are needed across systems now, and building pipelines for every source first is the blocker.
During migrations or M&A, when data lives in two estates and consumers should not have to care.
Data cannot move — residency, sovereignty, or contractual limits keep it in place, but analysis is still required.
The long tail of rarely-queried sources does not justify pipelines; federate the tail, centralize the hot paths.
when_not_to_use: Dashboards hit the same joins hourly — repeated federated scans cost more than one pipeline; centralize into an ELT stack (2).
Sources are fragile production databases that cannot absorb analytical scan load, and no replicas exist.
Sub-second latency is expected — cross-source planning and network hops set a floor no tuning removes.
Query results must be perfectly consistent point-in-time across sources — federation reads each source live and cannot freeze them together.

hot_spots.title: Source load
hot_spots.detail: Analytical scans hammer operational databases; without replicas or resource limits, federation incidents become production incidents.

hot_spots.title: Pushdown cliffs
hot_spots.detail: When a predicate cannot push down, the engine pulls whole tables over the network — the same query runs in seconds or hours depending on plan shape.

hot_spots.title: Semantic mismatches
hot_spots.detail: Types, collations, and timezone handling differ per source; joins succeed but return subtly wrong results.

hot_spots.title: Governance bypass
hot_spots.detail: Row policies defined inside each source do not travel — the federation layer must re-enforce them or it becomes the leak.

evolution.reason: Centralize the hot query paths into a warehouse when repeated federated scans outgrow their cost.

stages.name: Federation engine
stages.role: Plans and executes single-dialect SQL across heterogeneous sources
stages.rationale: Trino is the reference federation engine — the widest connector set and battle-tested pushdown; Athena is its serverless AWS form, Dremio adds reflections (built-in acceleration).

stages.name: Unified catalog
stages.role: One schema and permission surface over all connected sources
stages.rationale: The engine needs one place to resolve schemas; pairing it with a discovery catalog keeps analysts from guessing which source holds what.

stages.name: Access governance
stages.role: Row filters and column masks enforced at the federation layer
stages.rationale: Per-source policies do not travel through connectors — enforcing masks and filters in the engine is what keeps federation from becoming the bypass.

stages.name: Acceleration
stages.role: Caches and materializations for the hot query paths
stages.rationale: Federate the long tail, materialize the hot paths — a small serving store for repeated dashboards keeps federated scan costs sane.

stages.name: BI + clients
stages.role: Dashboards and ad-hoc SQL speaking one dialect to everything
stages.rationale: Consumers connect once to the engine instead of once per source — that single connection is most of the product.
